text: An IP address gets traffic to the right device. A port number gets it to the right application on that device. A single server can run a web server, a mail server, and a database all at once, all at the same IP address — the port is what tells the operating system which service should receive a given piece of traffic.

A handful of port numbers are worth memorizing cold: 22 for SSH, 25 for SMTP, 53 for DNS, 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS, 3389 for RDP. These are all well-known ports, 0 through 1023, reserved by IANA for a specific standard service — which is why a firewall rule referencing port 443 unambiguously means HTTPS traffic.

A well-known port is only half the story. When your laptop connects to a web server on port 443, it picks a random, temporary ephemeral port, typically in the 49152 to 65535 range, for its own side of that connection. The connection is then uniquely identified by the full combination: source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port.

This is why firewall rules always name well-known ports, never ephemeral ones — you can't write a useful rule around a port that's different every single time. Knowing HTTP is 80 and HTTPS is 443 cold lets you immediately test the right thing when troubleshooting, instead of guessing.

That closes out Chapter One, Networking Fundamentals. Chapter Two moves into Network Infrastructure & Services — switches, routers, DNS, DHCP, NAT, and basic firewall concepts, building directly on everything you just learned.
